name: The Hungry House
epithet: The Model Home at 13 Crystal Street

inspiration.oldScript: The haunted house that drives the father mad and destroys the family.
inspiration.newLens: The suburban facade itself: a model home that eats anyone who won't keep up appearances, learned from the woman paid to perform a perfect life inside it.

logline: 13 Crystal Street has been for sale since 1959 and has never looked better. Let your lawn go brown or your voices get loud, and you will get an invitation to its open house. Nobody who RSVPs comes home.
backstory: In 1959 Larkspur Homes finished Crystal Street and staged number 13, the Starlight Deluxe, as its model home, right down to the plastic fruit. To sell the dream, developer Dale Prescott hired Marjorie Vail to live in it as the hostess: from nine to six she baked cookies, vacuumed already-clean carpet and smiled at touring couples while two child actors played her kids on weekends. Her contract said she could not cry, receive visitors or keep her own things in sight. Her paintings went in a hall closet. Prescott refused to ever sell the model, because "people buy the dream, not the house." In the spring of 1963 Marjorie stopped coming out, and the doors were locked from inside. When Prescott's men broke in, the cookies were warm, the carpet had fresh vacuum lines, and Marjorie was gone except for the smiling portrait over the mantel. The house had learned her rules too well. Every Halloween week since, some family on Crystal Street that lets the facade slip receives an engraved invitation, and the hallway at 13 gains one more perfect photograph.

centralIssue.title: The perfect house that hides a person
centralIssue.summary: The house learned hunger from Marjorie Vail, who was paid to perform a flawless life until the performance swallowed her. It punishes mess because nobody ever let her have any. Find out who Marjorie really was and show the house that a home is a place where people are allowed to fall apart.

poster: A spotless pastel split-level model home glowing at the end of a dark cul-de-sac, its front door a smiling mouth, framed family photographs floating out of its windows like moths, a woman in a 1959 apron silhouetted in the bay window, a teenager on the sidewalk holding a crumpled engraved invitation
portrait: Close portrait of a 1959 housewife with a lacquered blonde flip and a fixed, too-wide lipstick smile, pearls, an apron, plastic fruit in her hands, her eyes wet and pleading while her mouth keeps smiling, a perfect living room fading into wallpaper behind her
endingPhoto: A spotless pastel split-level model home at the end of a cul-de-sac at night, its front door yawning open into a warm golden glow like a mouth, a welcome mat curling like a tongue, floating framed family photographs drifting from the windows, a woman in a 1959 apron smiling in the bay window, teens on bikes braking hard on the lawn
taunts: Wipe your feet, dear. We don't track the world in here.
Your family looks so tired. Wouldn't you rather look happy?
Every room is ready. We only need you to stop making a mess.
Smile. Smile wider. There. Now hold it forever.

clues.title: The hostess film
clues.hint: The library's local history room keeps the old Larkspur Homes papers, film reels and all.

encounter.title: Box 13 of the Larkspur Papers
encounter.place: Local history room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
encounter.text: The Larkspur Homes donation fills a wall of gray archive boxes. Box 13 is heavier than the rest. Inside: a 16mm reel labeled THE STARLIGHT DELUXE: A HOME FOR HAPPINESS, 1959, a typed hostess contract with coffee rings, and a little brass doorknob wrapped in a napkin like a sandwich. The old film projector in the corner is already plugged in.
encounter.art: A local history room in a small public library, a wall of gray archive boxes, a teenager lifting the lid of one heavy box to reveal a round 16mm film reel tin, a typed contract with coffee rings and a small brass doorknob wrapped in a paper napkin, an old film projector plugged in on a cart in the corner under a dusty green lamp, warm lamp light and dust in the air, medium shot

choices.label: Thread the projector and watch the promo film

success.text: The film flickers onto the wall: a smiling woman pulling cookies from an oven while a narrator says "Mrs. Vail loves every minute." You step through it frame by frame. Between two smiles, for exactly one frame, Marjorie looks straight into the lens and mouths: Let me out.
success.art: A flickering 16mm film projected on a library wall showing a 1959 housewife in a model kitchen, the film frozen where she stares into the camera mouthing a silent plea

failure.text: The film jams and the frame starts to bubble and burn. In the melting picture, the model kitchen is not empty anymore: you are standing in it, in an apron, smiling. The projector clicks off on its own and the reel is rewound when you check.
failure.art: A melting film image on a library wall showing a teenager in an apron smiling in a pastel 1959 kitchen, the projector bulb fading out

choices.label: Read the hostess contract line by line

success.text: HOSTESS WILL SMILE AT ALL TIMES WHILE THE HOME IS OPEN. HOSTESS WILL NOT RECEIVE PERSONAL VISITORS. HOSTESS'S PERSONAL EFFECTS, INCLUDING HOBBY MATERIALS, WILL BE STORED OUT OF SIGHT. In the margin, in pencil, a small neat hand has written: What if I am not happy, Mr. Prescott?
success.art: A typed 1959 employment contract under a library lamp, rules about smiling at all times, a tiny penciled question in the margin, a teenager's finger tracing it

failure.text: The contract is forty pages of real-estate legalese and you get lost around clause nine, "Carpet Maintenance." When you look up, the brass doorknob has rolled across the table and is resting against your hand, warm, as if someone was holding it a second ago.
failure.art: A brass doorknob resting against a teenager's hand on a library table covered in contract pages, a long shadow of a doorway falling across them

choices.label: Slip the reel into your backpack and watch it at home

success.text: You smuggle the reel past the desk and watch it on Toby's projector in a garage full of bikes. In the last scene, Marjorie opens a hall closet to hang a coat. The camera cuts away fast, but not fast enough: the closet is full of wild, bright paintings.
success.art: A teen crew in a cluttered garage watching an old film projected on a bedsheet, the frame showing a closet bursting with colorful paintings

failure.text: The security tag shrieks at the door. The reel is confiscated and you are banned from the local history room until Monday. As you leave, the library's front doormat reads WELCOME HOME in a script you have never seen before.
failure.art: A library security gate flashing red as a teenager is caught with a film reel, a doormat at the entrance reading welcome home in old-fashioned script

clues.title: The Night Owl Line tape
clues.hint: KGLM has archived every call to its overnight request line since 1961. Somebody called from 13 Crystal Street.

encounter.title: Caller from Thirteen
encounter.text: The KGLM tape archive is a closet of reel-to-reel boxes stacked to the ceiling, each one labeled in grease pencil. THE NIGHT OWL LINE, APRIL 1963 has a sticky note on it: CALLER FROM 13 CRYSTAL. DO NOT AIR. Somewhere above you the on-air light buzzes red, and the request line begins to blink, though nobody is on shift.
encounter.art: A cramped radio station tape closet stacked to the ceiling with flat reel-to-reel tape boxes marked in grease pencil, one box pulled out with a bright yellow sticky note on its lid, a teenager holding it, and down the hallway a red on-air bulb glowing and a request-line phone blinking on an empty desk, dim bulb light and red glow, medium shot

choices.label: Thread the reel on the booth deck and listen

success.text: A tired woman's voice whispers at 2:14 a.m.: "My face won't stop smiling. I try to stop and it won't. The house wants the kitchen clean when I'm crying in it." The 1963 DJ asks her name. "Marjorie. I used to paint. Is that silly?" Then a sound like a door closing very gently.
success.art: A reel-to-reel deck spinning in a dark radio booth, a teenager in big headphones listening with wide eyes, the needle of a VU meter twitching

failure.text: The tape stretches and warps. Marjorie's voice slides down into something slow and syrupy and not quite human: "Please wipe your feet." Every reel in the closet starts spinning at once, and you leave the station with the hallway feeling longer than it was.
failure.art: A wall of reel-to-reel tapes spinning by themselves in a dark station hallway, a frightened teenager backing away, magnetic tape curling through the air

choices.label: Pick up the blinking request line

success.text: Static, then an old woman in Oakland who says she listens every night. "My sister Marjorie called this show once, before she vanished. She painted the sky green and the dog purple. The man who owned the house said it upset buyers." She is crying, and so are you.
success.art: A teenager holding a radio station telephone receiver in a red-lit booth, a cassette recorder taped to the handset, tears in their eyes

failure.text: A pleasant woman's voice says, "Thank you for calling. Your family has been selected for a private showing." When you hang up, there is a cream-colored envelope on the console with your address in perfect script. It is not sealed yet.
failure.art: A cream envelope with an address in perfect script resting on a radio console beside a telephone, red on-air light reflecting off its gold edge

clues.title: Marjorie's trunk
clues.hint: A moving truck nobody hired dumps a load at Rusty's Junkyard every November. The oldest pile is in the back.

encounter.title: The Imperfect Pile
encounter.text: Behind the crusher is a mound of things somebody did not want seen: a lamp with a cracked shade, report cards with C-minuses, a ratty recliner, a box of sympathy cards, a mohawk wig dyed green. Joey says a white moving truck with no driver drops a load every year and the plates are from 1959. At the very bottom sits a steamer trunk stenciled M. VAIL.
encounter.art: A junkyard mound behind a car crusher heaped with ordinary family clutter, a lamp with a cracked shade, a ratty recliner, a shoebox of old greeting envelopes, a green-dyed mohawk wig, school papers with red marks, and at the bottom an old steamer trunk with stenciled initials, a lean Diné teenager in an orange work shirt and a teenager pulling at the trunk, a driverless white 1950s moving truck parked in the fog behind them, gray overcast light, wide shot

choices.label: Dig the trunk out before the pile shifts

success.text: You haul the trunk free and pop the latches. Inside are rolled canvases: a purple dog, a green sky, a self-portrait of a woman laughing so hard her lipstick is smeared. Under them, a stack of letters to her sister, all stamped, none of them ever mailed. The last one says: I'm going to stop smiling now.
success.art: An open steamer trunk in a junkyard spilling bright unrolled paintings of a purple dog and a laughing woman, a bundle of unmailed letters tied with ribbon

failure.text: The pile slides. You end up under a recliner and a lifetime of other people's embarrassments, and when Wade digs you out, the trunk is gone. A fresh tire track leads to the gate, and you smell cookies baking in the middle of a junkyard.
failure.art: A teenager pinned under a slumped recliner in a junk pile, a metalhead friend pulling them out, fresh truck tracks leading toward a foggy gate

choices.label: Start with the newest pile and see who it took

success.text: The newest things belong to the Brennan family, taken last Halloween: a divorce paper, a kid's broken trophy, a frying pan with a burned bottom. Every pile is somebody's normal bad day. At the bottom of all of them, under everything, Marjorie's trunk is full of the one thing she was never allowed to show: her own art.
success.art: A teenager kneeling in junkyard clutter holding a child's broken trophy and an old frying pan, a trunk of paintings visible underneath, sunset light through crushed cars

failure.text: The newest pile has your family's stuff on top: the mug with the chipped handle, the drawer of dead batteries, the photo where everyone's eyes are closed. None of it was thrown out. Not yet. You stand there a long time feeling sick.
failure.art: A teenager staring at their own family's chipped mug and blurry snapshot sitting on top of a junkyard pile, cold dusk light

signature.title: Open House, Tonight Only
signature.text: At eleven p.m. a sign appears on the lawn at 13: OPEN HOUSE, TONIGHT ONLY. The porch light is on, the door is ajar, and the whole street smells of chocolate-chip cookies. A woman in an apron waves from the bay window with a smile that does not move at all. Your feet are already on the welcome mat.
signature.art: A spotless pastel split-level model home at eleven at night, a small wooden realtor stake with red ribbons on the striped lawn, warm golden light spilling from the half-open front door, a 1959 housewife with a lacquered blonde flip, pearls, an apron and a fixed lipstick smile waving from the bay window, a teenager standing on the welcome mat with one foot raised, cookie-sweet golden light against a dark blue street, medium wide shot

choices.label: Go in and be the most polite guest it has ever had

success.text: You compliment the drapes, the shag, the plastic grapes. The house purrs. While it preens, you notice a hairline crack in the plaster by the coat closet, and someone has written in it, tiny, with a fingernail: I painted here once. You slip out before the cookies finish.
success.art: A teenager politely admiring a spotless 1959 living room, a tiny handwritten message visible in a hairline crack beside a coat closet

failure.text: You say something about the lamp being "kind of dated." The front door shuts with a soft, final click, and the hallway is suddenly much, much longer. It takes you until three a.m. to find a window.
failure.art: A teenager in an impossibly long pastel hallway lined with identical framed family photos, the front door tiny and far away behind them

choices.label: Stomp through the foyer in your muddiest sneakers

success.text: You moonwalk mud across the white carpet and leave a grape-soda can on the coffee table. The walls shudder like a disgusted aunt. The house spits you out onto the lawn and slams the door so hard the open house sign falls flat.
success.art: A teenager moonwalking muddy footprints across a pristine white carpet while the walls of a 1959 living room recoil in disgust

failure.text: The carpet drinks your footprints before you lift your feet. Then it drinks your shoelaces. You hop home barefoot, and in the morning your sneakers are on your porch, spotless, laced, with a note: We cleaned these for you.
failure.art: A pair of eerily spotless sneakers on a doorstep at dawn with a folded note tucked into one, a teenager staring at them barefoot

choices.label: Pull up the sign and tell the house you are not buying

success.text: You yank the sign out of the lawn and throw it in the street. "Not interested!" The porch light flickers off, offended. Down the block, three neighbors who were sleepwalking toward 13 in their bathrobes stop, blink and wander home.
success.art: A teenager hurling an open house sign into a dark street while sleepwalking neighbors in bathrobes stop on the sidewalk and blink awake

failure.text: The sign will not come out. It is rooted, warm, faintly pulsing. As you tug, the welcome mat under your feet slides an inch toward the door, then another, like a tongue.
failure.art: A welcome mat sliding like a tongue toward an open doorway, a teenager clinging to a rooted open house sign on a lawn at night

signature.title: The Family Portrait
signature.text: You come downstairs for water and the photos on your own walls have changed. Your family is in every frame, smiling with perfect teeth, wearing sweaters nobody owns. You are not in any of them. The hall carpet has turned pale mint, and from the kitchen comes the sound of someone humming while she wipes a counter that is already clean.
signature.art: A 1980s suburban upstairs hallway after midnight, every framed photo on the wall showing the same family in matching pastel sweaters with identical smiles and an empty gap where one child should stand, pale mint carpet spreading across the old brown carpet, a teenager in pajamas holding a glass of water, and at the end of the hall the kitchen doorway with the silhouette of a woman in an apron wiping a counter, dim hall light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Wake everyone up and make your family be themselves, loudly

success.text: You bang on doors. Someone burns toast at one a.m., someone argues about the thermostat, someone laughs so hard they snort. In every frame, the perfect smiles crack into real faces, and one by one, you appear in the pictures, mid-blink and gloriously unflattering.
success.art: A messy family kitchen at one in the morning, burnt toast smoking, people in mismatched pajamas laughing and arguing, framed photos on the wall changing to candid, blurry, joyful snapshots

failure.text: They will not wake. They lie in bed smiling with their eyes closed and their hands folded. The humming in the kitchen gets closer. By dawn the spell lifts, but for the rest of the day your family keeps saying "isn't this nice" in voices that do not sound like theirs.
failure.art: A family asleep in a dim bedroom with folded hands and identical serene smiles, a teenager shaking a shoulder in vain, a humming apron silhouette in the doorway

choices.label: Fake the perfect family dinner to fool it

success.text: You set the table with the good plates, put on a cardigan and say "Pass the peas, Father" to an empty chair. The humming stops, satisfied. The mint carpet rolls back like a tide. You have bought yourself one night and learned that the house can be flattered.
success.art: A teenager in a cardigan sitting at a formal dinner table set for a family of empty chairs, a mint carpet retreating out the door like a tide

failure.text: Your smile slips for one second. The plates rearrange themselves. The chairs fill with your family, and every one of them is smiling at you, waiting for you to smile back the right way. You do not sleep at all.
failure.art: A family seated rigidly at a formal dinner table, every face fixed in the same wide smile, all turned toward a frightened teenager at the head

choices.label: Pull every frame off the wall and turn it face down

success.text: Frame after frame goes face down on the carpet. With nothing left to look at, the hallway sighs and turns back into your hallway: scuffed baseboards, a lopsided school photo, a crayon mark from when you were five. You have never loved it more.
success.art: A teenager stacking face-down picture frames on a scuffed hallway carpet, a lopsided school photo and an old crayon mark visible on the restored wall

failure.text: Under each frame you pull down is another frame, and another, a wall of perfect photos all the way down. Glass slices your thumb on the last one. In that picture, finally, you are there: smiling in a sweater, standing in a hallway that is not yours.
failure.art: Layers of framed family photographs stacked endlessly on a wall, a teenager with a cut thumb staring at one photo showing themselves in a stranger's sweater

signature.title: Turn Your Back
signature.place: Mrs. Varga's kitchen, Crystal Street, house-sitting at midnight
signature.text: You are house-sitting for Mrs. Varga across the street while she visits her sister, and her kitchen is a glorious disaster: dishes in the sink, a cereal box on the stove, the cat's bowl upside down. You turn your back for one second to fill the cat's water. When you turn around, every kitchen chair is stacked on the table in a perfect, impossible tower, the dishes are gone, and the counter shines. Out the window, the porch light at 13 is blinking on and off, like it is winking at you.
signature.art: A gleaming 1980s kitchen at midnight, every kitchen chair stacked upside down on the table in a tall balanced tower, the counters shining empty, a teenager in a sweatshirt holding a cat's water bowl with a stunned face, a tabby cat on the floor, and through the window over the sink a porch light across the street blinking in a pastel house, white overhead light, medium shot

choices.label: Pull the chairs down and make a glorious mess on purpose

success.text: You unstack the chairs, dump the silverware drawer, spread the Sunday funnies across the floor and build a peanut-butter-and-pickle sandwich with maximum crumbs. Across the street, the porch light at 13 stops winking and goes dark in a sulk. The kitchen stays messy, which is to say it stays Mrs. Varga's.
success.art: A grinning teenager in a gloriously messy 1980s kitchen at midnight, chairs back on the floor, silverware and newspaper comics scattered everywhere, a crumb-covered sandwich in hand, a dark house visible through the window

failure.text: Every time you pull a chair down, you blink and it is back on top of the tower. By three a.m. the dishes are washed, dried and put away in alphabetical order. Mrs. Varga comes home to the cleanest kitchen she has ever owned and looks, for some reason, terrified.
failure.art: A spotless gleaming 1980s kitchen with chairs balanced in an impossible tower on the table, an exhausted teenager slumped against the counter, a cat staring up at the tower

choices.label: Turn your back again, and watch in the toaster's chrome

success.text: You face the sink and watch the shiny side of the toaster. In its curved reflection, a woman in an apron glides around the kitchen behind you, wiping, stacking, straightening, her smile fixed and her eyes wet. You whirl around and she is gone, but now you know: whatever cleans this street is not happy doing it.
success.art: A teenager staring into the curved chrome side of a toaster on a kitchen counter, the reflection showing a woman in a 1959 apron gliding behind them with a dishrag, her smile fixed and her eyes wet

failure.text: In the toaster's reflection, the woman in the apron is right behind you, very close, looking at your messy hair. A cold hand smooths it down, once. You drop the water bowl and do not stop running until you are on your own porch.
failure.art: A curved chrome toaster reflecting a smiling woman in a 1959 apron standing right behind a startled teenager, a dropped water bowl splashing across the kitchen floor, a cat bolting away

choices.label: Call Mrs. Varga and tell her the kitchen misses her

success.text: You call her sister's number in Sacramento. Mrs. Varga answers, sleepy, and you tell her the house is lonely and the dishes miss her. She laughs, cries a little, and admits nobody has seen her kitchen since the divorce. "Leave the dishes. I'll be home tomorrow." Behind you, very softly, the chair tower topples over.
success.art: A teenager on a kitchen wall phone with a long curly cord at midnight, smiling gently, a tower of chairs toppling over behind them, a cat curled on the windowsill

failure.text: The line clicks, and a voice that is definitely not Mrs. Varga's says, "This is Larkspur Homes. The owner is unavailable. Would you like to schedule a showing?" Every cabinet door in the kitchen swings open at once, perfectly stocked.
failure.art: A pale teenager holding a kitchen wall phone receiver at arm's length at midnight, every cabinet door in the kitchen swung wide open on rows of perfectly arranged identical cans and boxes

signature.title: One Minute on the Lawn
signature.place: The front lawn of 13 Crystal Street, 2 a.m.
signature.text: The dare is simple: stand on the lawn of 13 Crystal Street for one full minute. Your crew watches from behind the Dombrowskis' station wagon. The grass under your sneakers is greener than any grass has a right to be, mowed into perfect diagonal stripes, and as you stand there the stripes slowly turn to point at the front door. The pink plastic flamingos swivel their heads. Upstairs, two windows light up at once, like eyes opening, and the porch steps settle into a smile.
signature.art: A teenager standing alone in the middle of a perfectly striped emerald lawn at two in the morning in front of a pristine pastel split-level model home, the mowing stripes curving to point at the front door, pink plastic flamingos turning their heads toward the teen, two upstairs windows lit at the same moment, friends peeking from behind a station wagon across the street, a single dandelion in a crack in the front walk, cold moonlight and warm window glow, wide shot

choices.label: Stand your ground and finish the full minute

success.text: You count out loud, one Mississippi at a time, while the house stares and the flamingos edge closer. At sixty you stare right back into those upstairs windows, and the house blinks first: the lights flicker off, the lawn stripes go crooked, and a flamingo falls over. Your crew loses their minds cheering.
success.art: A teenager standing defiantly on a striped green lawn at night, two upstairs windows of a pristine split-level house flickering dark, a pink plastic flamingo tipping over, friends cheering behind a station wagon

failure.text: At forty-two the sprinklers snap on and swivel to face you, spraying water that smells like lemon floor polish. The flamingos herd you toward the porch, and you only escape by diving over the hedge, dripping and fragrant. You smell like a clean kitchen for two days.
failure.art: A soaked teenager diving over a trimmed hedge at night as lawn sprinklers spray them, pink plastic flamingos clustered on a perfect lawn, a pristine house glowing behind

choices.label: Rearrange the lawn ornaments into the tackiest display in California

success.text: You line the flamingos up in a conga line, give a garden gnome your sunglasses, and drape your flannel over the mailbox like a cape. The house makes a sound like a vacuum cleaner choking on a sock. Every blind upstairs snaps shut in disgust, and the lawn stripes go wobbly. You win the dare and, honestly, the night.
success.art: Pink plastic flamingos arranged in a conga line on a perfect suburban lawn at night, a garden gnome wearing sunglasses, a flannel shirt draped over a mailbox, upstairs window blinds snapped shut on a pristine house

failure.text: Every ornament you move slides back into place the second you let go. Then the gnome in your hand smiles, a little too wide, and you drop it and run. The next morning there is a gnome on your own front step, facing your door.
failure.art: A smiling ceramic garden gnome sitting on a suburban front step at dawn facing a closed front door, dew on the welcome mat, a perfect lawn across the street

choices.label: Kneel and protect the one dandelion growing through a crack in the walk

success.text: There is exactly one flaw: a dandelion pushing up through a crack in the front walk. You cup your hands around it and pour your water bottle over its roots. Upstairs, the eye-windows soften. For a moment a woman in an apron stands in one of them, palm flat against the glass, looking at the weed like it is the most beautiful thing she has ever seen.
success.art: A teenager kneeling on a pristine front walk at night cupping a single yellow dandelion growing from a crack, an upstairs window glowing with a woman in a 1959 apron pressing her palm to the glass

failure.text: The house notices what you are looking at. With a sound like a zipper, the crack in the walk seals itself, and the dandelion is simply gone. Upstairs the windows blaze brighter, and the porch steps curve into a wider smile.
failure.art: A teenager kneeling on a flawless sealed concrete walk at night, a pristine split-level house above with two blazing upstairs windows and porch steps curved like a wide smile

signature.title: Get Out
signature.text: You wake up because your room is clean. Not tidied: clean. Everything on your walls hangs perfectly level, your clothes are folded into squares, your comics are boxed and labeled, and you are tucked into a bed you did not make, with hospital corners so tight you can barely breathe. The room smells like lemon polish and warm cookies. From the heating vent, a woman's voice whispers, urgent: "Get out. Get out while it still thinks you're tidy."
signature.art: A teenager tucked rigidly into a perfectly made bed with tight hospital corners in a spotless 1980s bedroom at three in the morning, clothes folded into exact squares on the dresser, comic books boxed in rows with neat tags, every picture frame hanging level, and a warm yellow glow seeping from a heating vent in the wall beside the bed, the teen's eyes wide and turned toward the vent, dim lamp light, medium shot

choices.label: Kick off the covers and wreck the room

success.text: You thrash until the hospital corners pop like buttons, then fling your folded laundry in every direction, knock everything on the walls crooked and dump the comics in a glorious heap. The lemon smell fades. The room becomes yours again: loud, cluttered and perfect in the only way that counts.
success.art: A triumphant teenager standing on a rumpled bed amid flying laundry and a heap of comic books in a 1980s bedroom at night, crooked rock-band pinups on the walls, sheets tangled everywhere

failure.text: The corners tighten like a sealed envelope. You lie there, pinned and wide awake, while out in the hall a vacuum cleaner goes back and forth, back and forth, until sunrise. At breakfast your family compliments your room, and you want to scream.
failure.art: A wide-eyed teenager pinned flat under impossibly tight bedsheets in a spotless 1980s bedroom at dawn, clothes folded in neat squares, the shadow of a vacuum cleaner under the door

choices.label: Whisper back into the vent: "Who are you?"

success.text: "Somebody who used to fold things," the voice says, "and hated every minute." She tells you a secret: the house cannot stand a door left open. You creep through your house propping every door wide, and the sheets loosen with a sigh. "Thank you," says the vent, and something in her voice almost laughs.
success.art: A teenager crouched by a bedroom heating vent at night whispering into the grille, warm light spilling through a row of wide-open doors down the hall behind them, loosened bedsheets trailing

failure.text: The vent breathes out warm air that smells exactly like fresh cookies, and your eyelids get heavy, so heavy. You wake at dawn in a pastel cardigan you have never owned, buttoned all the way to your chin.
failure.art: A drowsy teenager waking at dawn in a buttoned-up pastel cardigan, curled on the carpet beside a heating vent, a tray of perfect cookies on the dresser, pale light through the blinds

choices.label: Grab a marker and relabel every box MINE

success.text: The house labeled everything, so you relabel it. MINE on the comics, the sock drawer and, for good measure, your own forehead. The room goes very still and confused, like a dog that has been told no. A model home only works while nobody owns it, and slowly the corners of the bedsheet let go.
success.art: A teenager in a 1980s bedroom at night scrawling on cardboard boxes with a fat black marker, a smudge of marker on their forehead, bedsheets slipping loose behind them, a lamp glowing

failure.text: The marker writes on its own, in neat cursive: DISPLAY ONLY. Every box, every drawer, your arm. You scrub until your skin is pink, and it does not come off until noon.
failure.art: A teenager scrubbing at neat cursive ink on their forearm at a bathroom sink in morning light, a fat marker on the counter, tidy stacked boxes visible in the bedroom behind

signature.title: The Rooms That Weren't There
signature.text: You fall asleep on your bed and wake on a sofa wrapped in plastic. You are inside 13, and it has grown: a nursery for a baby who was never born, a den where a TV plays the 1959 promo film on an endless loop, a staircase that goes up into more staircase. At the end of the hall, from inside a coat closet, someone is knocking. Three soft knocks. Then three more.
signature.art: The inside of a 1959 model home grown impossibly large, a teenager sitting up on a sofa covered in clear plastic, an empty pastel nursery visible through one doorway, a den where a boxy television plays a black-and-white film of a smiling woman, a staircase that climbs up into more staircase, and at the end of a long daisy-wallpapered hall a coat closet door, warm lamp light fading into shadow, wide shot down the hall

choices.label: Walk down the hall and open the closet

success.text: The closet is not a closet. It is a tiny studio with a window, paint on the floor, canvases everywhere, and a woman in an apron sitting very still on a stool with a brush in her lap. "I'm not allowed in here during showings," Marjorie whispers. "But it's the only room that's mine."
success.art: A tiny secret art studio hidden inside a coat closet, paint-spattered floor and bright canvases, a 1959 housewife on a stool clutching a paintbrush, looking up in surprise

failure.text: Inside is only coats, rows and rows of them, and they are all your size. One of them has your name sewn into the collar. The door closes behind you and you spend the rest of the night in the dark, listening to the house hum.
failure.art: A teenager trapped in a dark closet full of identical coats in their size, a name label on one collar, a thin line of warm light under the door

choices.label: Follow the wallpaper pattern back to the front door

success.text: The daisies on the wallpaper repeat every eighteen inches, except in one place where the pattern is upside down, like it was hung by someone in a hurry. You follow the wrong-way daisies down three halls and out the front door into cold, wonderful night air.
success.art: A teenager shining a flashlight along daisy wallpaper, one strip hung upside down, leading through a maze of pastel hallways to an open front door

failure.text: You follow the daisies until they follow you back. The pattern crawls across the ceiling and closes over the doorway like ivy. You wake in your own bed with the smell of wallpaper paste in your hair.
failure.art: Daisy-patterned wallpaper peeling off the walls and crawling over a doorway like ivy, a teenager backing away in a dim pastel hall

choices.label: Unplug the den TV and stop the promo film

success.text: You yank the cord. The film dies mid-smile, and for a second the whole house goes quiet, like an actor who forgot their line. In the silence, very far away, you hear a woman laugh, a real laugh, and the staircase sets itself back down to one floor.
success.art: A teenager yanking a television plug from the wall, the screen collapsing to a white dot, a looping staircase settling back into an ordinary single flight

failure.text: The TV keeps playing unplugged. The narrator's voice changes: "And here is our newest family member." On screen you are pulling cookies out of an oven, beaming. You pull the cord again and again until the dream lets you go.
failure.art: An unplugged television still glowing in a dark den, showing a teenager in an apron smiling in a 1959 kitchen, the real teenager holding the dangling cord

signature.title: Welcome Wagon
signature.text: At midnight your doorbell plays a chime it does not know. On the welcome mat sits a perfect lime gelatin mold on a paper doily, wrapped in plastic, with a card in flawless cursive: Welcome to the neighborhood! Do come to our open house. Fondly, 13. You have lived on Crystal Street your whole life. Suspended inside the gelatin, wobbling gently, are things from your own house: the spare key, your library card, the friendship bracelet you lost in fourth grade.
signature.art: A shimmering lime gelatin mold on a white paper doily sitting on a suburban welcome mat at midnight, wrapped in clear plastic, a house key, a small laminated library pass and a braided friendship bracelet suspended inside the green gelatin, a teenager in pajamas crouching in the doorway to look at it, a pastel model home glowing gold across the street, yellow porch light, close medium shot

choices.label: Walk the dish back to 13 with a polite thank-you note

success.text: You carry it across the cul-de-sac and set it on the porch of 13 with a note in your messiest handwriting: Thanks, but we like our house the way it is. As you turn to go, the door opens two inches, and a hand in a yellow rubber glove takes your note instead of the dish and holds it close, like something precious. You walk home with the gelatin, and the spare key slides right out.
success.art: A teenager setting a lime gelatin mold on the porch of an immaculate model home at night, the front door open a crack, a hand in a yellow rubber glove reaching out to take a folded note

failure.text: The porch of 13 is warm under your feet, like a tongue. The door swings open, and the smell of fresh cookies pulls at you so hard that you set down the dish and take two steps inside before you grab the doorjamb and wrench yourself back.
failure.art: A teenager gripping a doorjamb and leaning back from the glowing open doorway of a perfect model home at night, wisps of warm cookie-scented air curling out, a gelatin mold abandoned on the porch

choices.label: Eat it on the lawn with your bare hands, as loudly as possible

success.text: You plop down on the lawn and eat lime gelatin by the fistful, slurping, getting it in your hair, digging out your spare key with a triumphant squelch. Across the street, every curtain at 13 snaps shut in horror. A neighbor comes out to see what the noise is and laughs so hard she has to sit down on her steps.
success.art: A grinning teenager sitting on a front lawn at night scooping lime gelatin with bare hands, green goo in their hair, a neighbor laughing on her steps, every curtain on a perfect house across the street snapping shut

failure.text: The gelatin tastes like lemon floor polish. You gag, and when you look down, your hands and sleeves are spotless, as if someone very thorough has wiped them clean, and a second card waits on your step: Manners, dear.
failure.art: A grimacing teenager on a front lawn at night staring at spotless hands, a neatly folded doily and a cursive card waiting on the porch step, a perfect model home watching from across the street

choices.label: Flip the card over and read the recipe on the back

success.text: The back of the card is a recipe, and it is not for gelatin: rise at six, smile at the door, no crying, no visitors, personal effects out of sight. Under it, in a shakier hand, someone has written, "Is anyone reading this?" You take the card inside and pin it to your corkboard where you will see it every day.
success.art: A teenager at a kitchen table at night studying a cursive recipe card under a lamp, a wobbling lime gelatin mold beside them, the card pinned next to concert stubs on a cluttered corkboard

failure.text: You flip the card, and the cursive keeps writing itself across both sides and then onto your hands: wipe your feet, sit up straight, smile. You scrub at the sink until three a.m., and your hands smell like furniture polish for days.
failure.art: A teenager scrubbing their hands at a kitchen sink at night, elegant cursive handwriting crawling up their wrists, a lime gelatin mold glistening on the counter, suds everywhere

signature.title: Emergency HOA Meeting
signature.place: The Crystal Street clubhouse, one a.m.
signature.text: A pastel flyer under every door calls an emergency meeting of the Crystal Street Homeowners Association at one in the morning, and somehow every grown-up on the street goes. You slip in the back. The neighbors sit in perfect rows of folding chairs, nodding in unison, while a voice from the clubhouse PA, warm as a home economics teacher, reads the complaints: the Ferreiras' brown lawn, Mrs. Varga's dishes, your family's loud Sunday arguments. "All in favor of sending them an invitation?" Every hand in the room rises at once, slowly, like puppets.
signature.art: A pastel suburban clubhouse room at one in the morning, perfect rows of neighbors in bathrobes and slippers on folding chairs all raising their right hands at the same moment with blank smiles, a refreshments table with a punch bowl and deviled eggs, a speaker box on the wall glowing warm yellow, a teenager peeking in from the back door, flat fluorescent light, wide shot from the back of the room

choices.label: Stand up and confess that your house is a mess, and ask whose else is

success.text: You climb on a folding chair and say it: "Our house is loud and messy, we fight about the thermostat, and I love it. Whose house is a mess?" There is a long, awful silence. Then Mr. Ferreira raises his hand, then Mrs. Varga, then nearly everyone, laughing in surprise, and the PA crackles into embarrassed static.
success.art: A teenager standing on a folding chair in a pastel clubhouse at night, neighbors in bathrobes laughing and raising their hands, a wall speaker crackling, a punch bowl and cookies on a side table

failure.text: You stand up, and every head in the room turns toward you at exactly the same speed. The PA thanks you for volunteering. You spend the rest of the night trying to leave a meeting whose doors keep opening onto more rows of folding chairs.
failure.art: Rows of neighbors in bathrobes turning their heads in perfect unison toward a startled teenager in a pastel clubhouse at night, an open doorway revealing endless rows of folding chairs

choices.label: Find the bylaws and call a point of order

success.text: You grab the HOA binder off the refreshments table and flip to the back. "Point of order: only homeowners can vote, and 13 Crystal Street has never been sold." The PA sputters, because a model home cannot vote and cannot chair a meeting either. The neighbors blink, stand and shuffle home in their slippers, wondering why they came.
success.art: A teenager holding up an open binder and pointing at a wall speaker in a pastel clubhouse at night, neighbors in slippers blinking and standing up from folding chairs, the speaker sputtering

failure.text: The bylaws are one rule repeated for two hundred pages in perfect typewriter print: Keep up appearances. The PA thanks you for reading so carefully, and your family's name moves to the top of the agenda.
failure.art: A dismayed teenager flipping through a thick binder of identical typewritten pages in a pastel clubhouse at night, neighbors in rows smiling politely, a wall speaker glowing warmly

choices.label: Raid the refreshment table and make the messiest scene possible

success.text: You knock over the punch bowl, juggle three deviled eggs, drop one, and grind the cookie crumbs into the carpet. The neighbors gasp, then giggle, and then Mrs. Varga throws a deviled egg back. The PA tries to restore order and is drowned out by the first food fight in Crystal Street history.
success.art: A chaotic food fight in a pastel clubhouse at night, neighbors in bathrobes flinging deviled eggs and cookies, red punch splashed across the carpet, a teenager juggling eggs on a folding chair

failure.text: Every crumb you drop vanishes before it lands, and the carpet drinks the punch right out of your sneakers. The neighbors applaud politely, as if you are the entertainment, and the meeting moves on to new business: you.
failure.art: A teenager holding a tipped punch bowl over a spotless carpet in a pastel clubhouse at night, neighbors on folding chairs applauding politely, crumbs disappearing in midair

signature.title: The Moving Van
signature.text: The night before Halloween, a moving van from Larkspur Homes backs down Crystal Street with its hazard lights blinking, and movers in gray coveralls, with faces as smooth as eggs, start carrying out everything that makes the houses look lived in. Drum kits, lava lamps, crayon drawings, an ugly plaid recliner, somebody's entire record collection. Behind them, the houses are being staged: plastic on the sofas, wax fruit in the bowls, smiling family portraits on the walls. The van is already half full, and its back doors are breathing.
signature.art: A boxy white moving van with blinking orange hazard lights backed up on a suburban street after midnight, movers in gray coveralls with smooth blank egg-shaped faces carrying a drum kit, a lava lamp and a plaid recliner out of the houses, the van's back doors gaping open and glowing warm inside, a teenager and a skinny boy in a backwards red cap running across a lawn, orange hazard light and blue night, wide shot

choices.label: Get every neighbor out to point at their things and say "That's mine"

success.text: You and Kev bang on doors until the street fills with people in bathrobes. "That's mine," says Mrs. Varga, pointing at the recliner, and it slides right off a mover's back; "That's mine," says Mr. Ferreira, about a truly terrible velvet painting. Every claimed thing comes home, and the van's doors shut on an empty space with a hungry sigh.
success.alone: You bang on doors until the street fills with people in bathrobes. "That's mine," says Mrs. Varga, pointing at the recliner, and it slides right off a mover's back; "That's mine," says Mr. Ferreira, about a truly terrible velvet painting. Every claimed thing comes home, and the van's doors shut on an empty space with a hungry sigh.
success.art: Neighbors in bathrobes on a suburban street at night pointing proudly at their belongings, a plaid recliner sliding off a faceless mover's back, a velvet painting floating home, a moving van sagging empty

failure.text: People come out, but they stand on their perfect lawns smiling politely, unable to say the words. The movers load the recliner, the drum kit and the records, and the van rolls off into the dark toward the junkyard road.
failure.art: Neighbors standing frozen with polite smiles on immaculate lawns at night, faceless movers loading a drum kit into a moving van, red taillights fading down a dark road

choices.label: Climb into the back of the van and throw everything out

success.text: You vault onto the bumper and start hurling things into the street: records, lamps, a ceramic poodle, a crate of comics. The movers cannot catch everything at once, the neighbors scramble to gather their stuff off the asphalt, and the van jerks, gags and coughs you out onto a pile of beanbag chairs.
success.art: A teenager in the back of a moving van at night flinging records, lamps and a ceramic poodle into the street, neighbors scrambling to catch them, faceless movers reaching too late

failure.text: The doors swing shut behind you, and the inside of the van is a showroom: a perfect living room, a plastic-covered sofa, a smiling portrait of you over the fireplace. You pound on the walls until dawn, when the doors finally open on your own driveway.
failure.art: A teenager pounding on the walls of a perfect 1959 showroom living room inside a moving van, a plastic-covered sofa, a smiling portrait of the teen over a fireplace, warm lamplight

choices.label: Let the air out of the van's tires before it can leave

success.text: You crawl under the bumper with Joey and unscrew every valve cap on the van. It sinks with a sad, wheezing sigh, too flat to go anywhere, and by sunrise the movers have faded like a bad dream, leaving the whole street's belongings stacked on the curb for their owners.
success.alone: You crawl under the bumper and unscrew every valve cap on the van, one tire after another. It sinks with a sad, wheezing sigh, too flat to go anywhere, and by sunrise the movers have faded like a bad dream, leaving the whole street's belongings stacked on the curb for their owners.
success.art: Two teens crouching by the flat tires of a sagging moving van at dawn, faceless movers fading into mist, drum kits, lamps and recliners stacked along the curb of a suburban street

failure.text: The tires refill with a cheerful hiss as fast as you let them out. One of the movers crouches and peers under the bumper at you with its smooth blank face, and you scramble backward into the street and keep going.
failure.art: A faceless mover in gray coveralls crouching to peer under a moving van at night, a frightened teenager scrambling backward across the asphalt, hazard lights blinking

finale.title: The Last Open House
finale.text: On Halloween night the house swallows the cul-de-sac. Every family on Crystal Street sits at one endless dining table in sweaters they do not own, smiling smiles they cannot drop. At the head of the table, in a 1959 apron, Marjorie Vail carves a roast that is made of wax, and the house speaks through her lipstick: "Everyone is so happy here. Nobody ever has to be seen crying again." The walls breathe in. The front door is gone.
finale.art: An endless 1959 dining room on Halloween night, every family from a suburban street seated at one long table in matching pastel sweaters with frozen smiles, plates of wax food, and at the head of the table a 1959 housewife with a lacquered blonde flip, pearls, an apron and a fixed lipstick smile with wet pleading eyes carving a wax roast, four teenagers in homemade Halloween costumes standing in the doorway, warm chandelier light, long wide shot down the table

choices.label: Tear the walls down from the inside

success.text: Plaster gives, then lath, then the whole dream. The walls fall outward like a stage set, and the families tumble onto the cold lawn in their own clothes, blinking. Behind you, 13 Crystal Street is a dark, hollow shell, and nobody can say where Marjorie went.
success.art: The walls of a model home falling outward like a collapsing stage set, families tumbling onto a cold lawn under the moon, a teen with a baseball bat in the rubble

failure.text: Every hole you punch in the wall is patched before your fist comes back, smooth and freshly painted. The house sighs, patient as a mother. A sweater settles over your shoulders.
failure.art: A teen punching a hole in a pastel wall that instantly patches itself smooth, a soft sweater floating down onto their shoulders

choices.label: Hand the house a signed contract and tell it it has finally been sold

success.text: You slap a forged deed on the table and hammer a SOLD sticker onto the sign through the window. The house freezes. It was built to wait for a buyer, and now it has nothing left to wait for. Its doors swing open, and the families walk out past it one by one.
success.art: A teenager slapping a forged deed on a dining table while a sold sticker glows on a lawn sign through the window, the house's doors swinging open

failure.text: The house reads the deed and checks your references. "This signature is smudged, dear." The paper turns into a perfectly folded napkin in your hands, and the table makes room for one more chair.
failure.art: A forged deed folding itself into a perfect dinner napkin in a teenager's hands, an empty chair sliding up to the table beside them

choices.label: Hang Marjorie's paintings over the perfect portraits and say her name

success.text: You hang the purple dog over the family portrait and the laughing self-portrait over the mantel. You play her voice from the tape. "Marjorie, you don't have to smile." Her mouth trembles, and for the first time in twenty-three years it falls. She cries, a real, ugly, wonderful cry, and every family at the table cries with her, and the house, finally allowed to be a mess, lets them all go.
success.art: A weeping 1959 housewife in front of a wall of wild, colorful paintings hung over formal portraits, families at a long table crying and hugging, teens in costumes holding up a laughing self-portrait

failure.text: The paintings slide off the walls as fast as you hang them. Marjorie's smile is held up by twenty-three years of rules, and one night's truth is not enough to lift them yet. Push harder.
failure.art: Colorful paintings sliding down a pastel wall as a smiling housewife watches helplessly, a teen reaching to catch a falling canvas

choices.label: Make a mess at its perfect table, the way you learned to on the first nights

success.text: The house tested you early, and you learned it cannot stand a single spill. So you knock the gravy boat over on purpose, put your elbows on the table and pass the wax roast the wrong way. A house built to host the perfect dinner stalls mid-breath, and every door springs open while it tries to remember the rules.
success.art: A teenager grinning with elbows on an endless dining table as gravy spills across the white tablecloth, families in matching sweaters gasping, a woman in a 1959 apron frozen mid-carve, every door flung open

failure.text: You spill the gravy, and a napkin wipes it up before it can spread. The house smiles through Marjorie's lipstick. It flinched, though, and you saw it; make a bigger mess.
failure.art: A spotless white tablecloth on an endless dining table, a napkin gliding by itself to wipe up a spill, a woman in a 1959 apron smiling fixedly at a teenager

choices.label: Make your family loud, the way you fought back when the house came into your own home

success.text: When the house came for your home and your street, you fought it with noise. You shove back your chair and start the loudest argument at the table, about the thermostat, and your family joins in, then every family, until the perfect walls crack under the racket and fall outward like a stage set. Everyone tumbles onto the cold lawn in their own clothes.
success.art: Families in matching sweaters shouting and laughing at a long dining table as the walls of a perfect house crack and fall outward like a stage set, a teenager standing on a chair leading the uproar

failure.text: You shout, but the room swallows your voice like thick carpet. Your family looks over, smiles politely and folds their hands. Shout again; they nearly heard you.
failure.art: A teenager shouting at a long dining table while families in matching sweaters smile politely with folded hands, plush carpet and pastel walls closing in

choices.label: Claim her paintings for her, the way you learned to claim what was yours the night before

success.text: The night before Halloween you learned the house only lets go of what somebody claims. So you open the closet studio and say it for her, about every canvas, the purple dog and the laughing self-portrait and the paint on the floor: "That's hers." Marjorie's smile trembles and falls, and she cries, a real, ugly, wonderful cry, and the house, finally allowed to be a mess, lets every family go.
success.art: A teenager holding up a painting of a purple dog in a cramped closet studio full of canvases, a woman in a 1959 apron weeping with relief, families rising from a long dining table, walls softening

failure.text: You open the closet and say it, but the paintings slide off the walls faster than you can claim them. Marjorie's smile is held up by twenty-three years of rules. Keep saying it; she is listening.
failure.art: Canvases sliding off the walls of a cramped closet studio, a teenager trying to catch them, a woman in a 1959 apron with a trembling fixed smile watching from the doorway

best.title: Excuse the Mess
best.text: At dawn Marjorie Vail unties her apron, drops it on the clean carpet, and walks out the front door with a canvas under each arm. The library hangs her paintings that winter, and her sister drives up from Oakland for the opening. The Larkspur sign finally comes down. In the spring, 13 Crystal Street is sold to a loud family with three dogs, a drum kit and a lawn they never mow on time, and the house has never sounded happier.
best.art: A woman in a 1959 dress with her blonde flip coming loose walking out the front door of a pastel model home at dawn with a rolled painting of a purple dog under each arm, her apron dropped on the white carpet behind her, teenagers and neighbors in rumpled Halloween costumes cheering on the lawn, pink sunrise light, wide shot

good.title: Not on the Market
good.text: The house goes dark and stays dark. The open house sign never comes back, and the families who vanished in the hallway photos come home with no memory of where they were. But 13 Crystal Street is still perfect, still for sale, still waiting. You never walk past it without wiping your feet.
good.art: A spotless dark pastel model home with every window black on a gray November morning, a realtor stake still standing on its striped lawn, a teenager on the far side of the street walking past and wiping their sneakers on the curb, flat gray light, wide shot

bittersweet.title: One Frame Left
bittersweet.text: You get out, and so does almost everyone. But when the police finally walk through 13, there is one photograph still hanging in the hallway: the family from the end of the street, smiling in matching sweaters. Their house goes up for sale in December. Sometimes, late at night, you are sure you hear them laughing politely from the end of the street.
bittersweet.art: A single framed photograph of a smiling family in matching pastel sweaters hanging alone in an empty pastel hallway, pale squares on the wallpaper where other frames used to hang, a police officer's flashlight beam falling across the photo from the doorway, dark house and white beam, medium shot

bad.title: A Home for Happiness
bad.text: On November first there is a new photograph in the hallway at 13: you, in a sweater you never owned, smiling perfectly beside a tray of cookies. The open house runs every Sunday now. Your crew takes the tour again and again, standing in front of your picture, trying to make you blink.
bad.art: A framed portrait of a teenager in a stranger's pastel sweater with a frozen perfect smile beside a tray of cookies hanging in a pastel hallway, three friends in jackets standing in front of it on a Sunday house tour staring up at it, a smiling realtor with a clipboard behind them, warm afternoon light, medium shot
